topic: Physical storage backends for billion-cell polyhedral mesh IR (HDF5, ADIOS2 BP5, Zarr v3, Arrow/Parquet, custom mmap container, openPMD model)
findings:
## Scope and evidence quality
I fetched primary specs and docs where reachable. Several searches turned up no published head-to-head benchmark on mesh workloads, and I found no ZFP/Blosc/zstd ratios on mesh connectivity. Those gaps are flagged [UNVERIFIED] or "no evidence found" below. Numbers are only those quoted from fetched pages.

## 1. Candidate-by-candidate

### HDF5 (current line 2.x; 2.0.0 released 2025-11-11, 2.2.0 listed later)
- 2.0.0 introduced file format version 4.0 and C11 compliance; Autotools were dropped and the CMake option is now HDF5_PROVIDES_PARALLEL (changelog mirror: https://dawn2.umd.edu/cwrf-bias-correction-env/share/CHANGELOG.md; HDF Group newsletter #207 https://www.hdfgroup.org/?p=26293). The 1.14 to 2.x format-compat story is not verified.
- **Parallel I/O:** MPI-IO is mature. VTKHDF, Exodus (via netCDF-4) and CGNS all use it, which makes HDF5 the de facto interchange layer for the formats we survey.
- **Parallel compression** (https://support.hdfgroup.org/documentation/hdf5/latest/_par_compr.html and https://www.hdfgroup.org/2022/03/parallel-compression-improvements-in-hdf5-1-13-1/):
  - Available since 1.10.2, and only with collective I/O.
  - Ranks with no data must still join the collective call.
  - When several ranks touch one chunk, HDF5 assigns an owner rank and the others send it their changes over MPI.
  - Best performance needs chunk-aligned, one-writer-per-chunk writes.
  - Reads of filtered datasets were historically independent. The HDF Group recommended independent reads for filtered data even after 1.13.1.
  - Chunk metadata management scaled poorly at about 8k MPI ranks and beyond.
  - Parallel datasets force early space allocation (H5D_ALLOC_TIME_EARLY).
- **Filters:** only deflate, shuffle, szip and fletcher32 are built in. Zstd needs an external plugin; a forum report notes ParaView cannot read such files (https://forum.hdfgroup.org/t/h5repack-and-gzip-version-1-14-6-vs-2-1/13747). Portability therefore needs a plugin-path or "no exotic filters" policy.
- **Subfiling VFD:** a middle ground between file-per-process and a single shared file. It is a build option (a 2.1.0 build config showed it OFF). A 2020 RFC says parallel compression in subfiles would need re-implementation (https://support.hdfgroup.org/releases/hdf5/documentation/rfc/RFC_VFD_subfiling_200424.pdf).
- **Cloud:** the ROS3 read-only S3 VFD exists (listed in the 2.2.0 notes). Chunk metadata lives in the file, so remote partial reads are possible but latency-heavy. Cloud-optimized HDF5 needs careful paged aggregation [details UNVERIFIED].
- **Rust bindings:**
  - `hdf5` (aldanor): requires HDF5 1.8.4 or newer. OpenMPI and MPICH parallel builds are "supported and tested". Thread safety comes from reentrant mutexes, so calls are serialized. The GitHub page showed no releases and no maintenance banner. Its release cadence is [UNVERIFIED] (https://github.com/aldanor/hdf5-rust).
  - `hdf5-metno` 0.15.0 is an actively maintained fork. It has a `have-parallel` feature with an optional mpi-sys dependency, and optional blosc-src, lzf-sys and zfp-sys filter dependencies (https://docs.rs/hdf5-metno/latest/hdf5_metno/).
  - Rust-side HDF5 means linking libhdf5 (a C build dependency) and a global-lock performance ceiling.
- **64-bit ids:** native int64/uint64 datasets, no issue. Exodus uses EX_ALL_INT64_DB for on-disk 64-bit maps, entity ids and bulk data, and EX_ALL_INT64_API for the in-memory API (https://sandialabs.github.io/seacas-docs/html/index.html). The Exodus compression options only apply to netCDF-4 files, with gzip default and level 1 "often sufficient".
- **Append/versioning:** not transactional. SWMR exists with restrictions. Schema evolution is ad hoc, through attributes.

### ADIOS2 BP5 (https://adios2.readthedocs.io/en/latest/engines/engines.html)
- BP5 was introduced in ADIOS2 2.8 and became the default in 2.9. It is a step-based, append-oriented format.
- On disk it is a directory `name.bp/` holding `data.0..data.M`, `md.0`, `md.idx` and `mmd.0`.
- Aggregation:
  - Four strategies: TwoLevelShm (default), EveryoneWritesSerial, DataSizeBased and EveryoneWrites.
  - EveryoneWrites is N-to-N and "does not scale".
  - Default is one aggregator per node, using a shared-memory segment (MaxShmSize default 4GB).
  - Optional writer rerouting is available.
  - StripeSize default is 4KB.
- Metadata:
  - Selective metadata aggregation is on by default, with a two-level fallback (OneLevelGatherRankLimit 6000).
  - ORNL says the two-level metadata format uses roughly 1/3 to 1/4 of the BP4 metadata size on E3SM. This is a vendor claim for one app (https://www.ornl.gov/news/adios-28-software-release-new-file-format/).
- BP5 has async write, step selection and append (AppendAfterSteps). Memory use can approach half of BP4's.
- The BP5 engine page documents no compression operators. Operators such as Blosc, ZFP and SZ exist at the ADIOS2 level (my background knowledge, not verified on that page).
- Strengths: HPC write throughput, streaming and staging. In openPMD-api's matrix it is rated "A", "scales to petabyte data: yes", "dataset deletion: no" (https://openpmd-api.readthedocs.io/en/latest/backends/overview.html).
- Weaknesses for us:
  - It is a library-defined format. Third-party readers other than ADIOS2 are essentially nonexistent.
  - There is no Rust binding I could verify. ADIOS2 is C++ with C, Fortran and Python bindings [UNVERIFIED for Rust].
  - It is MPI-centric.
  - Random sub-array reads of one huge static array are not its design center. It is optimized for write-heavy time-stepped output.
- I found no published BP5 vs HDF5 numbers in my searches, only the openPMD-api rating and the ORNL claim.

### Zarr v3 (core spec 3.1; https://zarr-specs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/v3/core/index.html)
- **Layout:** a tree of groups and arrays. Each node has a `zarr.json`. Chunk keys look like `foo/baz/c/1/0`.
- **Array metadata:** zarr_format, node_type, shape, data_type, chunk_grid, chunk_key_encoding, fill_value and codecs are mandatory. attributes and dimension_names are optional.
- **Codec chain:** exactly one array-to-bytes codec, with optional array-to-array and bytes-to-bytes codecs around it.
- **Extension rule:** extensions are must_understand by default. 3.1 adds a `must_understand:false` escape hatch for codecs, storage transformers and attributes, but not for data types, chunk grids or chunk key encodings.
- **Store abstraction:** get, get_partial_values, set, set_partial_values and list_prefix. It maps directly onto POSIX, S3 and GCS.
- **Sharding** (`sharding_indexed`; https://zarr-specs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/v3/codecs/sharding-indexed/index.html):
  - A shard packs inner chunks plus an index. The index is uint64 [offset, nbytes] pairs with a crc32c checksum, at the start or end of the shard.
  - An empty inner chunk is 2^64-1 in both fields.
  - Inner order is unspecified, and gaps are allowed.
  - A reader reads the index first, then range-requests the chunk bytes.
  - Write strategies are fixed-order in place, or append-only with the index rewritten.
  - A shard is one object, so concurrent writers must be shard-aligned or coordinated. An NVIDIA Earth2Studio backend buffers whole shards for this reason. No MPI write guidance was found in the spec.
- **Irregular chunking:** variable chunking is draft ZEP 0003 and not yet core. Strings are ZEP 0007. This matters because mesh arrays (ragged connectivity, per-part ranges) are naturally irregular. We would use 1-D arrays with regular chunks plus our own offset arrays.
- **Rust: `zarrs`** (https://github.com/LDeakin/zarrs): claims conformance with Zarr 3.1 and implements many registered and draft extensions. It has a pluggable storage crate and a filesystem store. Its README gives no async information or numbers, and I did not see a crate version.
- **Throughput evidence:**
  - Zarrista (built on zarrs) reports 1.9x to 2.7x faster reads than zarr-python for compressed and compressed-plus-sharded data, and parity with TensorStore (self-reported beta; https://developmentseed.org/zarrista/latest/).
  - A Pangeo post claims zarr-python with Icechunk/Obstore saturates the EC2-S3 network and beats TensorStore and TileDB (https://discourse.pangeo.io/t/new-cloud-tensor-i-o-benchmarks-zarr-is-fast-now/5459). Date and sharding use [UNVERIFIED].
  - An IPDPS 2020 cost-model paper on Lustre found Zarr's file-per-chunk layout pays MDS open costs versus HDF5's single file (https://sdm.lbl.gov/~sbyna/research/papers/2020/2020-IPDPS-Kang-pred-comp-array-libs.pdf). Sharding mitigates this.
  - No MPI-scale mesh benchmark exists.
- **Versioning:** Icechunk adds ACID transactions, immutable snapshots, tags, and per-commit storage of only modified chunks, all on top of Zarr (https://icechunk.io/en/latest/overview/). Its Rust implementation and spec compatibility are not confirmed on that page.
- **Weakness for HPC:** no standard MPI-collective writer. Parallelism means "each rank writes its own shard/chunk files". Compression codecs (zstd, blosc) are standardized in the zarr-extensions registry, which is better than HDF5 plugins.

### Apache Arrow / Parquet / Feather
- **Arrow columnar format** (https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/Columnar.html):
  - List offsets are int32; LargeList uses int64 offsets, and a 1e9-cell polyhedral mesh needs LargeList. Offsets reference a child array, which is exactly a CSR layout.
  - Buffers are padded to 8 bytes, with 64 bytes recommended.
  - The IPC file format has a footer with schema and batch offsets for random access. It is relocatable, with no pointer swizzling, so it is mmap-friendly.
  - Extension types go through `ARROW:extension:name`, with fallback to the storage type.
- **Parquet** (https://parquet.apache.org/docs/file-format/): row groups, column chunks and pages, with the footer written last. It is built for tabular, nullable, columnar data with single-pass writing and column pruning.
- **Crates:** arrow-rs (arrow, parquet, arrow-flight). It officially supports only little-endian platforms. The version is around 59 to 60 (monthly releases; https://github.com/apache/arrow-rs). object_store moved to its own repository.
- **Fit:** poor for N-D dense, MPI-parallel HPC output, with no MPI-IO. Parquet's page-level compression does not suit random access to a CSR slice by index. It is good for tables (provenance logs, attribute tables, region membership, overlap tables). It is not a good primary store for the mesh arrays.

### Plain mmap-able custom container (safetensors-like)
- **safetensors** (https://github.com/huggingface/safetensors) has a very simple layout:
  - 8-byte little-endian u64 N, then an N-byte UTF-8 JSON header, then a raw byte buffer.
  - The header maps each name to dtype, shape and data_offsets.
  - The header is capped at 100 MB. The buffer has no holes and no overlaps. Data is little-endian and row-major.
  - It has no file-size limit.
  - Benefits: zero-copy mmap on CPU, lazy per-tensor loading, no code execution.
  - A BLOOM load across 8 GPUs went from about 10 minutes to about 45 seconds (their claim).
  - It has no chunking or compression, and the whole file is one append-unfriendly blob.
- **Gaps for us:** no groups or hierarchy, no chunk compression, no parallel write protocol, no checksums, no schema versioning. Sub-byte dtype alignment is not defined.
- **A custom container would need us to reinvent** parallel write coordination, compression framing, integrity checks, third-party readers and tooling. It wins on mmap zero-copy for the solver's hot path.

## 2. openPMD as the model (https://github.com/openPMD/openPMD-standard/blob/latest/STANDARD.md)
- **Standard** (version 1.1.0, dated 2018): required root attributes are openPMD (the version), openPMDextension (a uint32 bitmask) and basePath (`/data/%T/`), with iterationEncoding and iterationFormat. Meshes and particles have fixed record schemas, with unitSI and unitDimension on every component. The only extension is ED-PIC.
- **Backend-agnostic by requirement:** the standard demands only groups, N-D homogeneous arrays and attributes. It explicitly allows constant components (value plus shape attributes).
- **Validator** (https://github.com/openPMD/openPMD-validator): `openPMD_check_h5` for the 1.1.* branch, version 1.1.0.6 on PyPI. It "can not validate 100%" of the standard. Writers must pass it, and readers reject files with errors but must accept warnings.
- **Backends in openPMD-api:** ADIOS2 (parallel, scalable), HDF5 (parallel, portable) and JSON (serial reference, human-readable). The existence of the JSON backend made the abstract model testable and debuggable.
- **Lessons:**
  - The validator is HDF5-only, so backend-agnosticism was only partially realized in the validator. We should validate the logical model, not the bytes.
  - Domain extensions are bitmasked.
  - The spec is small and the abstraction is layered: a standard defines groups, arrays and attributes, and backends implement them.
  - The serial JSON backend is cheap and valuable as a golden reference.

## 3. How existing mesh formats lay out polyhedra (evidence for our schema)
- **VTKHDF** v2.8 (https://docs.vtk.org/en/latest/vtk_file_formats/vtkhdf_file_format/vtkhdf_specifications.html):
  - Unstructured grids are stored as one concatenated dataset per array across partitions, one partition per rank.
  - Per-partition NumberOfPoints, NumberOfCells and NumberOfConnectivityIds let each reader compute its slice offset.
  - Polyhedra use FaceConnectivity, FaceOffsets, PolyhedronToFaces and PolyhedronOffsets, so faces can be shared.
  - Id width follows the stored dtype.
  - This is essentially our face-first CSR, already proven with parallel HDF5 on a "concatenate partitions, with a count table" scheme.
- **Exodus:** 64-bit via DB and API flags, with netCDF-4/HDF5 gzip. Topology or geometry changes force a new file.
- **CGNS:** NGON_n/NFACE_n with ElementStartOffset (my background knowledge; my fetch of the SIDS page failed with 404 and I did not confirm cgsize_t there).

## 4. Compression
- No benchmark of Blosc, ZFP or zstd on mesh connectivity was found.
- Generic evidence: Blosc has a delta filter and a shuffle+delta filter. Blosc without shuffle is basically zstd. Custom reorder and delta filters beat Blosc defaults on float data (https://aras-p.info/blog/2023/03/02/Float-Compression-8-Blosc/).
- ZFP is lossy-oriented for floats and can do lossless integers, so it is generally a poor fit for connectivity.
- Unverified expectation: sorted-ish CSR offsets and local ids compress well with delta plus byte-shuffle plus zstd. We should measure this on our own meshes before choosing defaults.
- Fields (fluxes) could use lossy ZFP or fixed-rate quantization, but it should be off by default for geometry or topology.

## 5. Synthesis and recommendation
No single candidate is best on every axis:
- **HDF5:** best tool and reader ecosystem, MPI-IO collective, a single file, and what Exodus, CGNS, VTKHDF and MED already use. Its weaknesses are parallel compression complexity, a global lock in Rust, plugin-dependent zstd, and weak cloud and versioning behavior.
- **ADIOS2 BP5:** best raw write scaling at large rank counts. Its weaknesses are an ecosystem of one and no verified Rust bindings.
- **Zarr v3:** best cloud and object-store friendliness, a simple spec with a clean Rust implementation (zarrs), standardized codecs, and sharding that gives partial reads. Its weaknesses are no MPI-collective story and irregular chunks still being a draft ZEP.
- **Arrow/Parquet:** best for tabular metadata only.
- **Custom mmap container:** fastest and simplest for solver loading, at the cost of everything else.

**Recommended layered approach:** define the logical IR as an abstract "named N-D array + attributes + hierarchy" model (as openPMD does), with three physical profiles:
1. **Archive/interchange profile: Zarr v3 on a local directory or object store, with sharding** (zstd and blosc codecs, crc32c). Implement it with `zarrs`. Cloud-friendly, append-friendly and diffable.
2. **HPC parallel profile: HDF5 (parallel, collective, chunk-aligned) via hdf5-metno or a C/MPI shim**, mainly for interoperability with Exodus, CGNS and VTKHDF tooling and for MPI-IO on Lustre/GPFS.
3. **Solver-native profile: a safetensors-style mmap container**, one raw file per part (a header with array names, dtype, offsets, 64-byte alignment, per-array crc), written by exporting from the other profiles. Each rank mmaps only its own part with zero copy.

Treat ADIOS2 as an optional future backend (as openPMD-api does) rather than a day-one dependency.

Reasoning for the hybrid: our consumer is a neutron-transport code. Its hot path is read-mostly, with each part mapped once and then processed repeatedly, which is exactly what an mmap container optimizes. The cold path is archive, exchange and cloud. A billion-cell mesh has far more connectivity ids than a solver wants to decompress per access.
design_implications: Specify the IR as an abstract storage model (hierarchy of groups; named, typed, N-D arrays; attributes; checksums) independent of bytes, as openPMD does. Ship three backends against it: Zarr v3 (archive/cloud), HDF5 (HPC/interop), and an mmap container (solver). Add a human-readable JSON backend for tiny golden test meshes and conformance tests.

Write the spec plus a validator that checks the logical model (names, dtypes, id widths, offsets monotonic, left/right face references in range, orientation invariants, classification links), not the bytes, so it runs on every backend. This avoids openPMD's HDF5-only validator (check_h5). Make it a CLI plus a Rust crate. Bitmask-style extension flags plus a version triple are worth copying from openPMD.

Pin all ids to explicit 64-bit on disk: u64 for global ids and cell/face/node indices, with an optional u32 'local id' profile inside a part when counts < 2^32. Store the width in the metadata. Never use platform-dependent int (Exodus needed EX_ALL_INT64_DB vs API flags; VTKHDF follows platform vtkIdType). Rust uses u64/usize explicitly. Offsets arrays (CSR) must be u64 even if indices are u32 (Arrow's int32 List offsets overflow at 2^31).

Store the face-first mesh as CSR/CRS arrays: cell_to_face_offsets (n+1), cell_to_face_ids with a signed or bit-packed orientation, face_to_node_offsets, face_to_node_ids, face_left, face_right, plus classification arrays. Mirror VTKHDF's per-part concatenation: one logical array per field, with a per-part count table (NumberOfCells, NumberOfFaces, NumberOfConnectivityIds) so each rank computes its slice offset and reads/writes it independently.

Make a 'part' the unit of I/O and of sharding. One part holds the CSR arrays for one partition including ghost records. Align Zarr shard boundaries and HDF5 chunk boundaries with part boundaries, so there is exactly one writer per shard/chunk. This avoids HDF5's chunk-owner MPI exchange and Zarr's read-modify-write of shared shards.

Use 1-D arrays with regular chunks and carry irregularity in our own offset arrays, since Zarr variable chunking (ZEP 0003) is still draft and sharding index entries are fixed 16 bytes/inner chunk. Pick inner chunk of roughly 1-4 MiB uncompressed (about 128k-512k u64 ids) and shards of roughly 64-256 MiB; treat these sizes as starting points to be tuned, since no mesh benchmark exists.

Keep geometry and topology compression lossless: delta plus byte-shuffle plus zstd (level 1-3) for index arrays, applied via Zarr codecs (zarr-extensions registry) and, in HDF5, via the built-in shuffle+deflate by default to avoid external-plugin portability problems (zstd in HDF5 needs a plugin; ParaView could not read it). Allow lossy ZFP/quantization only for field data and only when the attribute says so. Benchmark compression ratios on our own connectivity before fixing defaults, since no public numbers exist.

In the mmap container, copy safetensors' simplicity: 8-byte header length, a JSON or CBOR header with name, dtype, shape, byte offsets and checksum per array, 64-byte aligned data (Arrow's recommended alignment, so SIMD loads work), little-endian, no holes, no overlaps, and a header size cap. Add what safetensors lacks: a magic number, format version, per-array crc32c, and a footer that allows append. Use memmap2 with unsafe-containment and validate the header before handing out slices.

Treat the container as immutable per snapshot and get versioning from the layout: content-addressed or copy-on-write arrays, a manifest listing the arrays in each snapshot, and a provenance log. On Zarr this is what Icechunk provides (immutable snapshots, tags, only-modified-chunks storage). We can either adopt Icechunk or mimic a 'manifest + immutable shards' scheme with the same semantics. Do not rely on in-place HDF5 mutation for history.

Schema evolution: write a format version and a per-layer schema version in root attributes. Unknown optional layers or arrays are ignorable (Zarr's must_understand:false semantics); unknown required ones must fail loudly. Keep layers (shape, topology, regions, mesh, interface records, fields, distribution, provenance) as separate groups so a reader can skip layers it does not need (e.g. the transport code ignores shape/B-rep).

Rust implementation plan: zarrs for Zarr v3 (the most mature pure-Rust option I found); hdf5-metno (maintained fork; has parallel feature flag) or a thin C shim for HDF5 collective I/O; memmap2 for the native container; arrow-rs/parquet only for tabular side tables (provenance, region membership, overlap tables, attribute tables), using LargeList/i64 offsets where lists are used. Note both Rust HDF5 crates serialize calls with a lock, so do not use many threads on one HDF5 file. Use MPI ranks for parallelism, or use Zarr/mmap per-part files for thread parallelism.

For objects and cloud: use the Zarr profile with sharding and byte-range reads, keep consolidated metadata small, and add a coalescing reader (zarr-python 3.3 merges ranges within 1 MiB gap, up to 16 MiB merged reads). Before committing, run a benchmark ourselves on a roughly 1e9-cell synthetic polyhedral mesh. Compare read of one part, write of N parts from N ranks, and cold S3 range reads across HDF5-parallel, zarrs-sharded and mmap. No such published mesh benchmark exists.

Do not adopt ADIOS2 BP5 as the primary format. It has the best published HPC write scaling story, but its readers/ecosystem are a single library, it has no verified Rust binding, and it is step-oriented. Keep the abstract storage model clean enough that an ADIOS2 backend could be added later, as openPMD-api did, if in-situ streaming or very large rank counts become a requirement.

Provide import/export converters to Exodus (EX_ALL_INT64), CGNS (NGON/NFACE) and VTKHDF from the IR. These are lossy views, since they cannot hold the cellular non-manifold topology, regions or provenance. Do not make them the native store.

corrections.claim: VTKHDF polyhedra (FaceConnectivity/FaceOffsets/PolyhedronToFaces/PolyhedronOffsets) 'is essentially our face-first CSR, already proven with parallel HDF5'.
corrections.correction: Overstated. VTKHDF (current version 2.8; polyhedron spec added in 2.5) is cell->faces->points with shared oriented faces ('a single (oriented) face can be used by multiple polyhedrons'); it defines NO face->(left,right)/owner-neighbour array. Only the per-partition concatenation scheme (NumberOfCells/NumberOfConnectivityIds, offset = sum of preceding partitions) is a proven precedent. The real face->cell precedents are CGNS ParentElements and OpenFOAM owner/neighbour (see missing_important).

corrections.claim: Keep topology compression lossless: 'delta plus byte-shuffle plus zstd ... applied via Zarr codecs (zarr-extensions registry)'; 'Compression codecs (zstd, blosc) are standardized in the zarr-extensions registry, which is better than HDF5 plugins.'
corrections.correction: No delta codec exists in zarr-extensions (17 registered codecs: bitround, blosc, bytes, cast_value, conditional, crc32c, gzip, n5_default, packbits, reshape, scale_offset, sharding_indexed, transpose, vlen-bytes, vlen-utf8, zfp, zstd) and zarrs 0.23.14 implements no delta codec; a standalone shuffle exists only as experimental 'numcodecs.shuffle' (shuffle is otherwise only inside the blosc codec). A delta step would be a custom must_understand codec, recreating the exact reader-portability problem the report flags for HDF5 plugins. Either do delta in-application before a registered codec, or drop delta from the default.

corrections.claim: 'Blosc has a delta filter and a shuffle+delta filter. Blosc without shuffle is basically zstd.'
corrections.correction: Misreads the cited blog. Blosc is a meta-compressor whose default is BloscLZ + shuffle (not zstd); the blog tested LZ4/Zstd as alternative inner codecs. Blosc's legacy 'Delta' filter 'is not a delta at all' (XOR since 2017) and shuffle+delta gave ratios 'below 2.0 everywhere'; the filter that works is Blosc2 >= 2.8 'bytedelta' placed after shuffle. Also Blosc defaults beat plain zstd on that float data. Whether the registered Zarr blosc codec exposes bytedelta was not checked.

corrections.claim: 'Rust-side HDF5 means ... a global-lock performance ceiling'; 'both Rust HDF5 crates serialize calls with a lock, so do not use many threads on one HDF5 file.'
corrections.correction: The ceiling is a libhdf5 property, not a Rust-binding flaw. A thread-safe libhdf5 build is a single global lock, and HDF5's CMake refuses HDF5_ENABLE_THREADSAFE with HDF5_ENABLE_PARALLEL: 'Parallel and thread-safety options are not supported, override with HDF5_ALLOW_UNSUPPORTED option' (same for HL, C++, Fortran). The crates' reentrant mutex is what makes a non-threadsafe (e.g. parallel) libhdf5 usable from threads at all. 'Use MPI ranks, not threads, for one HDF5 file' holds for every language.

corrections.claim: 'Parallel datasets force early space allocation (H5D_ALLOC_TIME_EARLY).'
corrections.correction: Only for UNFILTERED datasets created in parallel. For filtered (compressed) datasets early allocation is optional and incremental allocation is the default ('still forced for datasets created in parallel that do not have filters applied to them'). Relevant at 1e9 cells: compressed parallel datasets no longer pre-allocate full uncompressed extent.

corrections.claim: HDF5 2.0.0: 'the CMake option is now HDF5_PROVIDES_PARALLEL'.
corrections.correction: The 2.0.0 notes say 'Renamed library state variables, notably HDF5_ENABLE_PARALLEL is now HDF5_PROVIDES_PARALLEL' (exported config/state variables). The configure/build option is still HDF5_ENABLE_PARALLEL; develop CMakeLists.txt gates on 'if (HDF5_ENABLE_PARALLEL)'. Confirmed from the official release page: 'New file format version (4.0) and compliance with the C11 standard', CMake-only (Autotools dropped); release dated 11 Nov (2025, between 1.14.6 on 2025-02-05 and 2.1.0 on 03 Mar 2026). Prefer this source over the dawn2.umd.edu changelog mirror.

corrections.claim: 'Filters: only deflate, shuffle, szip and fletcher32 are built in.' and 'a forum report notes ParaView cannot read [zstd] files'.
corrections.correction: HDF5's built-in filter table also lists N-bit and scale-offset; gzip and szip are 'Optional Built-in' filters that depend on zlib/szip at build time. The cited forum thread is actually about an HDF5 2.1.0 build WITHOUT zlib in which 'h5repack -f GZIP=1' silently did nothing because GZIP is applied as an optional filter — i.e. even 'built-in' deflate is not guaranteed present, and optional filters are skipped silently. topic: Integrated project stores persisting geometry + mesh + association (Cubit .cub/.cub5, CGM, iGeom/iMesh/iRel/Lasso, Salome HDF, Simmetrix, ESP/CAPS, libMeshb/MMG)
findings:
**Evidence-quality note.** Verified items were read from source or docs in this session: libMeshb source and TeX spec, MMG header, MOAB `Tqdcfr` and deprecated `iRel_Lasso`, Cubit 16.06 help pages, the Lasso page, the Salome copy-mesh doc, and the ESP help page. Items marked [UNVERIFIED] come from memory or secondary hits. Primary details for .cub5, Simmetrix, Salome HDF and CAPS were not retrievable.

## 1. Cubit .cub / .cub5

**Verified: legacy .cub layout (MOAB `Tqdcfr.hpp/.cpp`, a reverse-engineered reader of .cub, https://bitbucket.org/fathomteam/moab, `src/io/Tqdcfr.*`):**
- The file is a custom binary container, not NetCDF or HDF5. It has a table of contents (`FileTOC`: endian, schema, numModels, modelTableOffset, modelMetaDataOffset, activeFEModel).
- A model table holds several "models", each with a `modelHandle` and `modelType`. Handle 1 with type 1 is the ACIS SAT model: an embedded ACIS SAT text stream, with offset and length.
- Each FE model has a header (`FEModelHeader`: endian, schema, compressFlag, length). It has seven array descriptors, each with count, tableOffset and metaDataOffset: geom, node, element, group, block, nodeset, sideset.
- A metadata container holds typed entries (owner, name, int/double/string/arrays). Examples are `DataVersion` and `CubitVersion`.
- Format versions change under the reader's feet: `data_version <= 1.0` shifts element-type enums (+4 for types >= 15), and there are block-record size differences (52 vs 55 bytes) for Cubit <14.1 vs >=14.9. A MOAB-dev commit message says the ACIS UNIQUE_ID attribute format changed in Cubit 14 (https://lists.mcs.anl.gov/pipermail/moab-dev/2014/006155.html). The takeaway is that there are schema-version hazards and reverse-engineering cost.
- Per geometry entity (`GeomHeader`: geomID, nodeCt, nodeOffset, elemCt, elemOffset, elemTypeCt, elemLength), the file stores the mesh nodes and elements owned by that geometric entity. Mesh is therefore stored per owning geometry entity (owner association by containment), with ids that tie it back to ACIS entities.
- The association key is a pair of ACIS attributes on each ACIS entity, parsed by `parse_acis_attribs`: `UNIQUE_ID`, `ENTITY_ID`, `ENTITY_NAME`, `COMPOSITE_ATTRIB ... UNIQUE_ID/ENTITY_ID`, `CUBIT_ID`. The association is geometry-side attribute -> id -> mesh-side owner record. Mesh does not hold a pointer to the B-rep.
- Blocks, nodesets and sidesets are separate headers listing element, node or (element, side) members. Sideset data differs between `data_version <= 1.0` and later versions (`Tqdcfr.cpp` ~L680-790).
- MOAB then represents this as entity sets tagged `GEOM_DIMENSION` (int, default -1) and `UNIQUE_ID`/`GLOBAL_ID`, plus `MATERIAL_SET` tags, i.e. classification as tagged sets (`src/MBTagConventions.hpp` L63-70).

**Cubit documentation (Cubit 16.06 help, fetched with curl -k):**
- Persistent attribute types are Color, Composite vg, Genesis entity (block, sideset and nodeset membership), Id, Mesh container ("handle to mesh defined for the owner"), Mesh scheme, Name, Partition vg, Smooth scheme, Unique Id ("used to cross-reference other entities"), Vertex type (for mapping and submapping), Virtual vg (https://www.sandia.gov/files/cubit/16.06/help_manual/WebHelp/geometry/attributes/persistent_attributes/attribute_types.htm).
- Attributes are written to and read from the solid-model file. `Set Attribute {On|Off}` controls them, and `Auto Actuate|Update` controls automatic restore and write. On import, attributes go into an intermediate representation and are "actuated" later onto entities (`.../attribute_commands.htm`).
- Virtual geometry (composite, partition, collapse, simplify) modifies topology "without affecting the underlying ACIS geometry". All operations are reversible, and the attributes `Composite vg`, `Partition vg` and `Virtual vg` restore it on load (`.../virtual_geometry/virtual_geometry.htm`).
- The Cubit manual says a .cub stores only the end state, not the construction history (journal files hold the process). This is from the 15.x/16.x import docs: https://www.sandia.gov/files/cubit/16.06/help_manual/WebHelp/geometry/import/geometry_import.htm (from the search snippet; the fetch failed on TLS).

**[UNVERIFIED] .cub5:** No primary description was found. My recollection, not confirmed here, is that Cubit 15+ writes a newer "cub5" container variant with the same logical model, using larger offsets and a newer metadata schema, and that Cubit remains the only full reader. Design conclusion: assume it is undocumented and proprietary, and do not plan to read it.

**Regeneration behavior (verified from docs):** Cubit has no reliable regeneration from a .cub. Remeshing re-runs commands (journal) or re-uses the stored Mesh scheme, Smooth scheme and Vertex type attributes on the geometry. After a geometry modification, Cubit's strategy is to make topology edits virtual (reversible) and keep mesh-intent attributes on entities. Associativity across a real geometry change relies on ACIS attribute inheritance via split, merge and copy callbacks [UNVERIFIED in this session].

## 2. CGM (Common Geometry Module)
- CGM keeps its own topology data structure on top of any modeler (ACIS, OCC, facet-based), so topology can be modified independently of the underlying modeler. It supports non-manifold topology and virtual geometry (Tautges 2001, https://unpaywall.org/10.1007%2FPL00013387, from the search snippet).
- Virtual entities (`CompositeSurface/Curve`, `PartitionSurface/Curve/Loop`, etc.) sit between the topology and the true geometry. Composite merges entities into one topological entity. Partition splits one, adding virtual vertices, edges and faces on the real underlying geometry. Both are recorded as `CubitAttrib` subclasses (`CAUniqueId`, `CAEntityId`, `CAGroup`, `CACompositeVG`, `CAPartitionVG`, ...), seen in cgm branch file listings (https://lists.mcs.anl.gov/pipermail/cgma-dev/2014/002569.html, https://lists.mcs.anl.gov/pipermail/cgma-dev/2010/001040.html).
- Persistence is "attribute on the entity, restored by actuation": each attribute has write, read, update and actuate hooks, with an ordering so unique-ID attributes actuate before virtual-geometry ones.

## 3. ITAPS iGeom / iMesh / iRel / Lasso
- iRel (https://sigma.mcs.anl.gov/lasso/what-is-lasso/) defines relations as "pairwise associations between entities or entity sets", created per pair of interfaces (e.g. iGeom <-> iMesh), so lower-level interfaces stay independent. A Relation Handle is returned, and set/get calls then assign and query relations.
- The relation types are `iRel_ENTITY`, `iRel_SET` and `iRel_BOTH`, defined for each side of the pair (`moab/deprecated/itaps/irel/iRel.h`). Each side is declared as entity-type or set-type, with an iRel_ACTIVE/PASSIVE flag [partial].
- Lasso (v3.0.0, March 2012) is the one implementation. It "can recover the associations between mesh and geometric model entities" from Cubit .cub files read into CGM and MOAB.
- Verified mechanism (`iRel_Lasso.cpp` ~L570-600): Lasso matches geometric entities to mesh entity sets by (dimension, id), where the mesh sets carry `GEOM_DIMENSION` and `GLOBAL_ID/UNIQUE_ID` tags, and then calls `set_relation`. The association is a pure id join, recomputed on load. It is not stored as a first-class relation. Hence the 2013 MOAB-dev remark that a key function is "restoring relations on existing data sets" (https://lists.mcs.anl.gov/pipermail/moab-dev/2013/005744.html). iRel is deprecated within MOAB (`moab/deprecated/`).
- Lesson: a typed, separate relation layer is clean for coupling independent libraries. Making it recoverable only by id join means identity stability is the whole game.

## 4. Salome (.hdf study) [mostly UNVERIFIED]
- Verified (https://docs.salome-platform.org/latest/gui/SMESH/_sources/copy_mesh.rst.txt): when a mesh is copied onto a modified geometry, hypotheses, sub-meshes and groups are rebound by sub-shape. If "a sub-shape used to define a sub-mesh, group or hypotheses is not found in the new geometry", the dependent object is marked red in the Object Browser. A group on geometry degrades to a standalone group (a plain id list), and "can't be transformed back" to a group on geometry. The doc does not say how old and new sub-shapes are matched.
- Forum reports (https://discourse.salome-platform.org/t/partition-an-already-existing-geometry-while-retaining-groups/1887) say groups and sub-meshes are lost when the geometry is re-partitioned.
- From memory, not checked: the study is one HDF5 file with a SALOMEDS tree, with each module component storing its own persistent string/stream. GEOM stores shapes as BREP streams plus a function/dependency graph for parametric rebuild. SMESH stores meshes, hypotheses (as parameter strings), algorithms, sub-meshes (keyed by shape entry plus sub-shape index in a `TopTools_IndexedMapOfShape`), and groups on geometry. Association is a study-tree reference (entry string) plus a topological sub-shape index. Indices break when the geometry operation changes enumeration.

## 5. Simmetrix (.smd / .sms) [UNVERIFIED, secondary only]
- Nothing in the search results documents the format. The PHASTA wiki shows a `.smd` model (plus a derived `.dmg` for classification) and `.sms` mesh pair (https://fluid.colorado.edu/wiki/index.php/Convert). The documentation ships with SimModSuite, not on the web.
- From PUMI/SCOREC usage and memory: the .sms mesh stores each mesh entity's classification as a (model entity dimension, tag) pair against the model's own persistent tags. Model entities carry persistent integer tags/ids, and attributes (BCs, mesh sizes) attach to model entities in the .smd by tag. Mesh and model are separate files linked only through those integer tags, and the model can be a native CAD file wrapped by a "discrete" or Parasolid model.
- Simmetrix GeomSim/MeshSim use "model-based" attribute cases to keep BCs on the model while remeshing freely.

## 6. ESP / CAPS attribute model
- ESP "maintains a set of global and local attributes on a configuration that are persistent through rebuilds. This association is essential in the support of multi-fidelity models" (ESP/CAPS papers, https://acdl.mit.edu/ESP/Publications/AIAApaper2022-2248.pdf; https://flexcompute.github.io/EngineeringSketchPad/EngSketchPad/ESP/ESP-help.html: "persistence of Attributes, even through regenerations"). The models are fully attributed, parametric solid models.
- CAPS reads face/edge/node attributes such as `capsGroup` (a string name grouping faces into BC/property groups), `capsMesh`, `capsBound`, `capsConstraint`, `capsLoad` and `capsIgnore`. Session slides show solver AIMs keyed by capsGroup name, e.g. `Wing` -> inviscid, `Farfield` -> farfield (https://acdl.mit.edu/ESP/archive/Training2021/CAPS/lectures/session08.pdf). The exact semantics of each attribute and the entity-name mapping were not verified.
- Association rule: attributes are authored on the parametric model, inherited by the B-rep through EGADS operations, and the mesh is regenerated from the attributed B-rep each time. Mesh-side groups are derived (capsGroup -> integer index -> boundary tag), never authored on the mesh. This gives regeneration by construction.

## 7. libMeshb / .meshb / MMG
- Verified from `libMeshb/sources/libmeshb8.c` keyword table and `Documentation/libMeshb7.tex` (https://github.com/LoicMarechal/libMeshb), including `VerticesOnGeometricVertices: ii`, `VerticesOnGeometricEdges: iirr`, `VerticesOnGeometricTriangles: iirrr`, `VerticesOnGeometricQuadrilaterals: iirrr`, `EdgesOnGeometricEdges: ii`, `TrianglesOnGeometricTriangles: ii`, `TrianglesOnGeometricQuadrilaterals`, `QuadrilateralsOnGeometricTriangles/Quadrilaterals: ii`, `Corners: i`, `Ridges: i` (edge index), `RequiredVertices/Edges/Triangles/Quadrilaterals: i`, `TangentAtEdgeVertices: iii`, `NormalAtVertices: ii`, `NormalAtTriangleVertices: iii`, `Tangents/Normals: r*d`, `SubDomainFromGeom: iii` (triangle, orientation +/-1, subdomain ref), `ReferenceStrings: iic`, `PeriodicVertices/Edges/Triangles/Quadrilaterals: ii`, `BoundaryLayers`, `Fault_*` diagnostics.
- The "geometric" in `*OnGeometric*` means a support (CAD-faceted) mesh, not a B-rep. The record is (source entity, support-mesh entity, barycentric coordinates in it, distance). It is not a CAD (u,v). The doc states "barycentric position on this edge/triangle/quad and the distance from it". So libMeshb classification is mesh-on-mesh projection data.
- There is no persistent B-rep topology identity in the file. Surface/edge identity is carried only by integer references on every element (the last int of Triangles/Edges), and by Corners/Ridges/Required tags on entities. The file format is a flat keyword/section stream (binary or ASCII, version 1-4 floats/ints widths).
- MMG (https://github.com/MmgTools/mmg, `src/common/mmgcommon_private.h` L145-175) tags points and edges internally with bit flags: `MG_REF` (reference edge), `MG_GEO` (geometric ridge), `MG_REQ` (required), `MG_NOM` (non-manifold), `MG_CRN` (corner). These are derived from the input file's Ridges/Corners/Required sections plus angle detection. Remeshing preserves required entities exactly and treats refs as boundaries to keep. Geometry is re-approximated via a Hausdorff-controlled cubic-Bezier surface fit built from the discrete mesh (`-hausd`), not by querying CAD. [Hausdorff and Bezier details from memory.]
- refine (NASA) and Feflo.a (Pointwise/Boeing-style) typically take an EGADS/CAD link (refine: `.meshb` plus `.egads` projections; each boundary node carries a face id and (u,v)) [UNVERIFIED in this session]. Feflo.a uses `.meshb` with `.solb` metric fields.

## Cross-cutting synthesis (what each persists)
| Store | Geometry persisted | Mesh persisted | Cross-layer association | Regeneration story |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cubit .cub | ACIS SAT embedded + virtual-geom attrs | per-geometry-entity node/element arrays | ACIS attribute ids (UNIQUE_ID/ENTITY_ID) joined to model-table owner records | end state only, re-run journal, virtual geometry reversible |
| CGM | any modeler + own topology + virtual layer | not owned | CubitAttrib on entities, actuated on read | attribute inheritance |
| iRel/Lasso | n/a | n/a | separate relation object between ITAPS interfaces, recovered via (dim,id) join | none, recompute |
| Salome HDF | BREP + op history | meshes, hypotheses, groups | study entry + sub-shape index | rebind by sub-shape, unmatched objects flagged red |
| Simmetrix | .smd model | .sms | integer (dim, tag) classification | remesh from model attributes |
| ESP/CAPS | parametric model + attributes | not primary (regenerated) | named attributes (capsGroup) | rebuild, attributes persist |
| libMeshb | none (optional support mesh) | flat sections | integer refs + barycentric projections onto support mesh | MMG remesh using Required/Ridge/Corner tags |
design_implications: Adopt three separate association mechanisms in the IR, since no existing store provides all three. (a) Authoring-side intent is attached by stable name/attribute to B-rep or topology entities (CAPS capsGroup, Cubit Genesis/Id attributes). (b) Classification is a first-class typed relation table, mesh entity -> (topology entity id, dim, optional parametric coordinates), in the style of Simmetrix/PUMI and libMeshb. (c) Provenance records link both to the producing generator version. Do not rely on Lasso-style recompute-by-id-join as the only truth.

Give every topology entity a persistent UUID-like or monotonically allocated identity, separate from its positional index. Persist an id-lineage map (old id -> new ids, with split, merge and delete reasons) across B-rep edits. This is the weakness shared by Cubit (UNIQUE_ID attributes broke across Cubit 14), Salome (sub-shape index fragile, unmatched objects turn red) and CGM. Persist the lineage in the provenance layer so regions, BCs and sizing intent can be rebound mechanically.

Make sizing intent, schemes and BC/material attributes live on the topology/regions layers (Cubit Mesh scheme/Smooth scheme/Vertex type attributes, CAPS capsGroup/capsMesh) and treat the mesh as a derived, reproducible cache. Store a content hash of the inputs (shape, topology, attribute, sizing) in the mesh record so staleness is detectable, and support partial invalidation: only the topology entities whose lineage changed.

Keep virtual topology (composite/partition) as a reversible overlay layer between shape and topology, as in CGM/Cubit, with explicit overlay records (kind, member ids, parametrization) persisted by the store. Mesh classification should point at the overlay (virtual) entity, with a pointer to underlying true entities for projection.

Store classification of mesh entities as (dim, topology id) for every entity, plus parametric coordinates (u, v or t) and a projection distance/tolerance for boundary vertices only. Libmeshb stores barycentric position on a support mesh plus distance. For a native kernel we should store true (u, v)/t on the B-rep and optionally a support-mesh barycentric fallback so we can export to meshb/MMG/refine workflows.

Serialize and export Corners/Ridges/Required/non-manifold as per-entity flag sets derived from topology and sizing intent (MMG MG_REF/GEO/REQ/NOM/CRN bit flags), not as the primary store. Our IR derives them from topology (vertices, sharp edges, user-locked entities, interface edges) and a 'locked' bit used by remeshing and by non-conformal interface records.

Containerization: do not use a custom offset/table binary container like legacy .cub, whose reverse-engineering cost and schema drift (data_version, per-version record sizes) are visible in Tqdcfr. Use a self-describing chunked container (e.g. HDF5/Zarr/or a Rust-native versioned columnar archive) with one group per layer, per-layer schema version, explicit array dtypes, and a manifest. Embed or reference the B-rep as an opaque, versioned blob plus a neutral export (STEP/BREP), since the ACIS SAT embedded in Cub is the main interoperability lock-in.

Keep relations as a separate typed layer, but with the relation stored, not recomputed. iRel-style relation (entity<->entity, set<->set, both) is a good API model. Persist the relation tables (topology id -> mesh sets and mesh entity -> topology id) explicitly and verify them against a (dim, id) join on load as a consistency check. This solves Lasso's 'restore relations' problem.

For neutron transport, make region/material/interface/boundary-set association first-class on the topology layer and persist cell->region assignment with the region version, so a geometry or mesh regeneration keeps material IDs stable. Also persist the CAPS-style named-group -> integer-tag map so exported cell/side sets are stable across regenerations, with a diagnostic flagging unmatched or orphaned groups (Salome red markers) rather than silently degrading to standalone groups.

Provide import/export adapters rather than imitating foreign stores: .meshb with *OnGeometric* sections (support-mesh projection) and Ridges/Corners/Required; Exodus blocks/sidesets from regions; a DAGMC/MOAB-style export using GEOM_DIMENSION plus GLOBAL_ID tagged sets for downstream Monte Carlo; and a Cubit reader only if a documented API becomes available.

Record a regeneration manifest (generator ids/versions, parameters, seeds, input hashes) in provenance so that a stored mesh can be reproduced bit-for-bit or re-derived on demand, addressing Cubit's 'end state only, replay journal' limitation. Optionally store an operation history (Salome GEOM style function graph) for parametric re-evaluation.

topic: CSG, universes/lattices, instancing and reactor meshing hierarchies
findings:
## Scope and reliability
Verified by fetching primary docs: OpenMC geometry.xml spec, MOOSE Reactor module generator docs (raw GitHub markdown, `next` branch), MOOSE CSGLattice doc via search snippet. Partly verified from search snippets only: the Griffin CMFD GCMR example, MCNP lattice behavior, GEOUNED/McCad/SuperMC. NOT verified (mooseframework.inl.gov, virtualtestbed.inl.gov and serpent.vtt.fi returned 403 to fetch; DAGMC JOSS PDF unreadable): the Serpent `lat` details beyond the search snippet, the DAGMC quantitative performance/accuracy numbers, Griffin CMFD internals, and which surface types McCad/SuperMC/GEOUNED support.

## 1. How MC codes represent geometry

**OpenMC** (https://docs.openmc.org/en/stable/io_formats/geometry.html), verified.
- **Surfaces:** each has `id`, `type`, `coeffs`, `boundary` (transmission | vacuum | reflective | periodic) and optional `periodic_surface_id`. Types are x/y/z-plane, general plane (A,B,C,D), x/y/z-cylinder, sphere, x/y/z-cone, x/y/z-torus, and a 10-coefficient general quadric.
- **Cells:** each has `id`, `universe` (default 0), `region`, and exactly one of `material` or `fill`.
  - `fill` is a universe id.
  - A material *list* gives distributed materials, so one cell definition has per-instance materials.
  - `temperature` can also be a list (distributed temperatures).
  - `rotation` (Tait-Bryan angles in degrees, R = Rz·Ry·Rx) and `translation` apply only to filled cells.
- **Region** is a boolean expression over signed surface ids. Space means intersection, `|` union, `~` complement. Precedence is parentheses, then complement, then intersection, then union.
- **Universes** are sets of cells that share a local coordinate frame.
- **Rectangular lattice:** `dimension` (2 or 3 ints), `lower_left`, `pitch`, `universes` (a row-major array of universe ids), and optional `outer` (a universe tiled outside the lattice; without it, leaving the lattice is an error).
- **Hex lattice:** `n_rings`, `n_axial`, `orientation` (x or y), `center`, `pitch`, `universes` listed ring by ring, and `outer`.
- **Lattice elements are references to universes, not copies.** Instancing is thus a first-class idea: the same pin universe is referenced by hundreds of lattice slots. Per-instance data is limited to distributed materials/temperatures (and tallies filtered by distribcell).
- **`dagmc_universe`:** loads an `.h5m` file (`filename`, `auto_geom_ids`, `auto_mat_ids`, `length_multiplier`).
  - Per-volume `<cell>` sub-elements override `material`, `temperature`, `density` and `volume` by DAGMC volume id.
  - `region`, `fill`, `translation` and `rotation` are NOT allowed inside the DAGMC universe.
  - A faceted universe is therefore a leaf that can be placed in a CSG hierarchy, but it is not itself instanced with transforms inside.

**MCNP** (search snippets from LANL reports; the manual was not fetched).
- Uses `U=` (universe), `FILL=` and `LAT=` on cells.
- A lattice cell has an index range, e.g. `FILL=-1:1 -4:4`, followed by the universe for each index.
- Universes are "essentially infinite, cropped by the cell they sit in".
- A universe reused in several places always has identical geometry, materials and densities. Per-instance material variation needs separate universes. This is a limitation relative to OpenMC distributed materials.
- MCNP6 requires a fill on every lattice cell.

**Serpent** (search snippet only).
- Lattices use the `lat` card, with 18 lattice types (square, X/Y hex, X triangular, infinite single-universe, and others).
- The root universe is "0".
- The typical 3-level nesting is core lattice → assembly lattice → pin.
- The docs warn that a universe with a very large number of cells performs poorly. (unverified detail)

**MOOSE CSG library** (CSGLattice doc, snippet).
- MOOSE now has an in-memory CSG representation with an abstract `CSGLattice` base.
- It ships Cartesian and regular hexagonal lattices.
- Derived lattices implement `getAttributes`, `isValidIndex`, `isValidUniverseMap`, `clone`, `setUniverses` and `compareAttributes`.
- A lattice is "a 2D universe map plus attributes (pitch, etc.) that cannot be derived from the map".
- Lattices are extensible via subclassing. Useful as a design reference because it separates the universe map from the geometric attributes.

**Common pattern across all codes.** A definition (universe) is separate from placement (a fill with transform, or a lattice slot). Lattices are regular index → definition maps with a pitch, and there is an `outer` fill for out-of-range. Boundaries are tagged on surfaces (vacuum/reflective/periodic). Materials are bound at the leaf cell (OpenMC may override per instance).

## 2. CAD-to-CSG and DAGMC

- **GEOUNED** (Catalán et al., Nucl. Eng. Technol. 2024, doi:10.1016/j.net.2024.01.052; García et al., Fusion Eng. Des. 168, 2021, doi:10.1016/J.FUSENGDES.2021.112366): converts CAD to MCNP/OpenMC, with PyPI metadata also listing Serpent and PHITS. It has an automatic **void generation** module, because engineering CAD does not model the empty space and Monte Carlo codes need every point of space to be in some cell. A 2026 KIT abstract describes parallel void generation on an ITER model. The exact decomposition algorithm was not verified.
- **McCad (KIT)** and **MCAM/SuperMC (FDS Team)**: both decompose solids into convex or primitive pieces and emit semi-algebraic (surface/region) models.
  - Search snippets say McCad's older version was weak in decomposition because of kernel instability. Newer decomposition is more robust (INIS record 232zd-e0k26).
  - MCAM decomposes into convex solids and maps them to SuperMC basic solids. v5.2 exports to MCNP, FLUKA, Geant4 and TRIPOLI.
  - Surface-type coverage (tori, B-splines) was NOT verified.
- **DAGMC** is faceted CAD: the geometry is a triangulated, ideally watertight surface mesh, with one surface mesh per CAD face, volumes, and groups for materials and boundary conditions.
  - It avoids the CSG conversion and void-generation burden.
  - Costs: curved surfaces become flat facets, so volume mismatches happen (OpenMC discourse thread suggests checking volumes before running). Watertightness is required.
  - An MIT SM thesis (dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/157233) compares CSG vs DAGMC speed/memory; its conclusions are "positive for DAGMC" but I did not retrieve the numbers.
  - The Frontiers MSRE paper (10.3389/fnuen.2024.1385478) compares CSG and CAD models.
- **Trade-off summary:** exact quadric CSG gives exactness, small memory, and fast hierarchical lattice traversal, but the CAD-to-CSG step is lossy and fragile (decomposition, void). Faceted DAGMC converts anything, but is approximate, needs watertight tessellation, and has no native instancing.

## 3. Reactor meshing hierarchies (MOOSE Reactor module)

All verified from raw MOOSE docs on GitHub (`modules/reactor/doc/content/...`).

**Pipeline.** `ReactorMeshParams` (global: `geom` = Square|Hex, `dim` 2|3, `axial_regions`, `axial_mesh_intervals`, `region_id_as_block_name`, `flexible_assembly_stitching`, `num_sectors_at_flexible_boundary`) → `PinMeshGenerator` → `AssemblyMeshGenerator` → `CoreMeshGenerator` (plus `ControlDrumMeshGenerator`). The lower-level, older generators are `PolygonConcentricCircleMeshGenerator`, `PatternedHexMeshGenerator`, `PatternedCartesianMeshGenerator`, `HexagonConcentricCircleAdaptiveBoundaryMeshGenerator`, `FlexiblePatternGenerator` and `AdvancedExtruderGenerator`.

**Pin.**
- `region_ids` is an axial-layer × radial-zone table (rings, then background, then ducts). Reusing a value gives the same region.
- Block IDs are auto-generated, with names like `RGMB_PIN<type>[_REG<region_id>]`.
- Extra element integers: `pin_type_id`, `region_id`, `plane_id` (axial layer). With `use_as_assembly` it also writes `assembly_type_id`.
- Boundaries: outer boundary id = 20000 + pin_type, named `outer_pin_<type>`. Top/bottom boundary ids come from ReactorMeshParams.

**Assembly.**
- Places 2D pins (extruded pins cannot be fed in; extrusion happens at assembly level) via the patterned generators.
- IDs: `assembly_type_id`, `pin_id` (assigned with `assign_type = cell`), `plane_id`, and `region_id` for non-pin elements.
- Duct: `duct_region_ids` is an A×D table (axial × radial) with `duct_halfpitch`. `background_region_id` is one per axial layer.
- Outer boundary id = 2000 + assembly_type, named `outer_assembly_<id>`.

**Core.**
- Lattice of assemblies (hex or Cartesian).
- Empty positions get dummy assemblies, later removed with `BlockDeletionGenerator`.
- Default stitching does not check node alignment (`flexible_assembly_stitching` enables non-matching assembly boundaries).
- Outer radial boundary named `outer_core`, top/bottom named `top`/`bottom`.
- Adds `plane_id`, `assembly_id` (dummies excluded), optional `depletion_id` (`pin`|`pin_type` for heterogeneous cores, `assembly`|`assembly_type` for homogenized), and periphery with `RGMB_CORE` block and `region_id`.

**Reporting IDs on Patterned* generators.** Set `id_name` (multiple allowed) with `assign_type`:
- `cell` (default): unique sequential per tile, numbered from the upper-left, left to right, top to bottom.
- `pattern`: tiles built from the same input share an ID.
- `manual`: from `id_pattern`, with `|` separating multiple patterns.
- `exclude_id` skips dummy regions. Ducts get IDs starting above the maximum lattice ID.

**Boundary/interface IDs.** Patterned generators use interface boundary IDs offset by 30500 (SLICE_ALT): even = inward, odd = outward, shiftable per tile via `interface_boundary_id_shift_pattern`.

**Key observation.** MOOSE meshes are **fully flattened**. Each pin placement is a copy of mesh elements (stitched). The hierarchy survives only as *integer tags* on elements (`pin_type_id` = definition, `pin_id`/`assembly_id` = instance, `plane_id`, `region_id`, `depletion_id`). Definition vs. instance is encoded as two different IDs (`*_type_id` vs. `*_id`). Memory is O(total elements). Docs do not describe any mesh reuse or instancing; I verified that absence for the Pin and Assembly pages. There is a `data_driven_generator` option (metadata-only mode) in AssemblyMeshGenerator docs.

**Reporting IDs are first-class** in the Reactor module: they feed per-region cross-section/material lookup in Griffin, depletion, and post-processing.

## 4. CMFD / coarse-mesh hierarchies (Griffin) - partially verified

From the GCMR assembly VTB example (virtualtestbed.inl.gov/microreactors/gcmr/GCMR_Multiphysics_models.html; the page returned 403 to fetch, so this is via search snippet):
- Griffin is given only the fine mesh (`Griffin_mesh.e`) and builds the CMFD coarse mesh in the input.
- Chain: `SubdomainExtraElementIDGenerator` (defines `material_id` and `equivalence_id` extra IDs per subdomain) → `GeneratedMeshGenerator` (the coarse grid) → `CoarseMeshExtraElementIDGenerator`, which writes `coarse_element_id` onto each fine element (the fine→coarse map is stored as an element integer on the fine mesh).
- KRUSTY example uses only `material_id`.
- HPMR-H builds three meshes (DFEM-SN transport, Bison thermal, CMFD acceleration) with the Reactor module.
- A slide-deck snippet says the coarse mesh carries XS/material IDs and flux/equivalence IDs (SPH equivalence).
- My fetch of the `CoarseMeshExtraElementIDGenerator` doc 404'd, so the exact semantics (geometric containment by centroid vs. otherwise) are unverified.

Concept: the coarse mesh is a *second, independent mesh* that is a geometric partition (usually a pin- or assembly-aligned grid), plus a fine→coarse integer map, plus a separate `equivalence_id` namespace controlling which regions share homogenization or SPH factors.

## 5. Answers to the design question

Should the IR support instancing and multi-level hierarchies? Yes. Reasons:
1. Every MC code treats definition/placement as fundamental (OpenMC universe/lattice, MCNP U/FILL/LAT, Serpent universes), so the first consumer (neutron transport, possibly MC) will want the same structure for tracking, tallies, and cross-section assignment.
2. MOOSE's flattened-plus-tags approach loses the definition/instance relationship and costs memory. For a full core (e.g., ~50k pins × ~10^2-10^3 elements per 2D pin cell x axial layers) the flat mesh is large, but a pin type is meshed once. (These numbers are illustrative, not measured.)
3. Deterministic transport (e.g., method of characteristics, and ray-tracing on a regular pin/assembly hierarchy) benefits from hierarchical ray tracing and from storing a pin's mesh once.
4. But FEM/FV solvers and partitioners want a flat view. So both a hierarchical (instanced) and a flattened (expanded) view must exist, derived deterministically from one another.

Caveat: instancing breaks when instances differ (distorted/deformed meshes, thermal expansion, non-matching assembly boundaries as with `flexible_assembly_stitching`, per-instance refinement). The IR needs a way to say an instance is "the same mesh with an affine transform plus attribute overrides", and a clean "unshare/flatten this instance" operation.
design_implications: Add an explicit 'definition vs. placement' pair to the topology/regions layers: `Prototype` (a self-contained sub-complex: B-rep or CSG fragment, mesh, local frame, named interface ports) and `Instance` (prototype ref + rigid/affine transform + attribute overrides). Borrow OpenMC semantics: fill references a universe, transform is rotation+translation, material/temperature overrides can be lists per instance (distributed materials).

Add first-class `Lattice` objects (Cartesian, hex with ring ordering and orientation, extensible like MOOSE CSGLattice): a 2D/3D index->prototype map plus separate attributes (pitch, center/lower_left, orientation, n_rings, n_axial) and an `outer` fill. Keep the universe map and the geometric attributes separate. Allow nesting to arbitrary depth (pin -> assembly -> core -> plant) and a sparse lattice (empty slots) instead of MOOSE-style dummy assemblies plus delete.

Represent hierarchy in the mesh layer as: one mesh per prototype (cell->face, face->(L,R), classification to topology) plus an instance table; define a deterministic `flatten(depth)` that expands instances into one global mesh with a stored mapping instance-path -> entity-ID range. Provide the reverse (`detect_repeats`) only as an optimization, not as an authoritative input.

Make the IDs MOOSE exposes first-class typed attributes rather than ad-hoc integers: distinguish `*_type_id` (prototype id) from `*_id` (instance id), plus `region_id`, `material_id`, `plane_id` (axial layer), and `depletion_id`/`equivalence_id` (user namespaces). Support the three MOOSE assignment policies (`cell` = unique, `pattern` = per prototype, `manual` map) and `exclude`. In the instanced representation these become derived from the instance path (hierarchical index tuple) with no per-element storage; in the flattened view they materialize as per-element integer fields.

Provide a per-prototype region_id table (axial layer x radial zone, like PinMeshGenerator region_ids and AssemblyMeshGenerator duct_region_ids) as a sizing/regions concept so the same radial zones can reuse region IDs across axial layers.

Treat the coarse/CMFD mesh as an independent mesh of the same topology with an explicit fine->coarse map stored as an integer field on fine cells (as Griffin does with coarse_element_id), and a separate equivalence namespace for homogenization/SPH. In the hierarchy, coarse cells should be definable by hierarchy level (pin, assembly, axial plane) as well as by an arbitrary grid; store the map on the instance path so it is O(instances) rather than O(elements) when meshes are shared.

Support non-conformal assembly interfaces natively: MOOSE only gets `flexible_assembly_stitching` with sector counts. Our non-conformal interface records and overlap tables should be keyed by instance-port pairs, and a prototype should declare its boundary ports (named outer boundary, e.g., 'outer_assembly_N') so stitching between instances is a recorded relation, not a geometry rewrite.

Keep boundary/interface naming and numeric-ID conventions out of the data model: MOOSE uses magic offsets (20000+pin_type, 2000+assembly_type, 30500 interface offsets, odd=outward/even=inward). Use named, hierarchical boundary sets plus a stable id allocator, with the numeric IDs generated only on export (Exodus).

Offer a CSG-flavored geometry front end as an alternative to B-rep: regions as boolean expressions over signed quadric surfaces (OpenMC syntax is a good textual interchange: `-1 +2 | ~(3)`), universes, lattices, boundary types (vacuum/reflective/periodic with paired surfaces). This gives exact import/export to OpenMC/MCNP/Serpent models, and lets the mesher mesh a CSG pin cell exactly.

Plan for two geometry export modes for an MC consumer: (a) exact CSG hierarchy export (OpenMC geometry.xml, MCNP U/FILL/LAT) from prototypes + lattices whenever the B-rep is analytic (planes, cylinders, spheres, cones, tori); (b) faceted DAGMC-style .h5m export from the mesh surfaces (watertight, with volume and group tags for material/BC), with an explicit volume-conservation report between B-rep and facets since facet volume mismatch is a known problem. Do not allow DAGMC transforms on instances unless exported as a separate universe (OpenMC forbids fill/rotation/translation inside a DAGMC universe).

Include a void/complement computation in the B-rep/topology layer (what GEOUNED does with its void generation module): the cellular complex must cover the whole domain, with an explicit 'void' region and an outer boundary, so that downstream MC export does not need a separate step.

Provide provenance on instances: record the generating pattern (e.g., ring-ordered hex pattern, lattice index) and prototype hashes so equal prototypes are deduplicated and 'assembly placed N times' round-trips. Use content hashes of prototype meshes to detect when an imported flat mesh (e.g., from MOOSE Reactor module Exodus with pin_type_id/assembly_id integers) can be re-compressed into prototype+instances.

Importer for MOOSE Reactor module Exodus: read element integers (`region_id`, `pin_type_id`, `pin_id`, `assembly_type_id`, `assembly_id`, `plane_id`, `depletion_id`, `material_id`, `equivalence_id`, `coarse_element_id`) and boundary names (`outer_pin_N`, `outer_assembly_N`, `outer_core`, `top`, `bottom`) into our attribute layer, as a compatibility target for the first consumer.

Define a hierarchical addressing scheme (path of lattice indices + prototype id) usable across IR layers for tallies/fields/distribution (distribcell-style), so that partitioning can assign whole assemblies to ranks and fields can be stored per prototype x instance without duplicating geometry.
